operationalization: From time-lapse of growing organs, compare the growth-rate anisotropy field with the orientation and timing of division planes, and with organ shape after divisions are reoriented or suppressed. The claim is supported if shape and division geometry are predicted by the growth field, and weakened if division orientation changes form while growth anisotropy stays fixed.

candidate_datasets.name: Image Data Resource
candidate_datasets.role: Public light-microscopy studies of dividing cells in growing plant and animal tissues, for aligning division planes with tissue strain.

candidate_datasets.name: BioImage Archive
candidate_datasets.role: Open cellular imaging, including developmental time series from which growth and division can be measured in model organs.

obstacles: Growth and division are mechanically coupled, so a correlation does not by itself settle which is cause.
Open imaging covers a few model organs, not growing multicellular structures in general.
rationale: Direction of causation can be turned into a comparison of strain and division, but only after choosing what counts as a decisive perturbation. Suitable movies exist for Arabidopsis, Drosophila and a few other systems, scattered across imaging archives rather than as one growth-versus-division table. That sample can test the relation in those organs and cannot cover the stated scope of plants and animals, and analysis means harmonizing datasets before any causal contrast is credible.

operationalization: Score published ultrastructure of spicules, cartilage, bone, concretions and plant cell walls for whether the first mineral lies in extracellular matrix or cell wall rather than in active cytoplasm. A high extracellular fraction supports the rule; a large class of intracellular precipitation refutes it as a rule.

candidate_datasets.name: Cell Image Library
candidate_datasets.role: Reviewed cell micrographs, including extracellular matrix and mineral skeletons, for locating crystals relative to cytoplasm.

candidate_datasets.name: EMPIAR
candidate_datasets.role: Open electron and X-ray tomography that can show whether mineral is inside cells or in surrounding formed material.

obstacles: Dead or inactive tissue is not a label in image archives and has to be inferred from cell integrity.
Intracellular calcification, as in coccolithophores, is well known but unevenly archived relative to vertebrate bone.
rationale: The site of precipitation is a standard ultrastructural observation, so the rule is directly scorable where images resolve mineral and cytoplasm. Those images are spread through papers and image archives, with bone and a few protist groups far better covered than spicules and plant walls. A compiled subset can support or damage the rule, but assembling a taxonomically fair sample is months of work rather than a download-and-test.

operationalization: In published lime-free versus normal seawater rearings of echinoid embryos, score skeletal-rod presence, larval-arm length and survival. Suppression of rods and arms with continued development supports the claim; normal skeletons, or death rather than skeleton-less development, refutes it.
obstacles: The rearings are reported as figures in papers, not as a reusable open table of larvae, treatments and phenotypes.
Apparently healthy is loosely defined, and the published experiments cover a few echinoid species rather than skeleton-forming organisms generally.
rationale: Rods, arms and survival are an obvious confirming and refuting pattern, and the contrast with seawater controls is discriminating. The observations exist in the experimental literature, including later repeats of calcium-free culture, but they are not gathered in a public dataset that can be reanalysed as data. A literature compilation can test the claim for the species that were reared and cannot underwrite the broader extension.

operationalization: Test two proxies: whether sunlight reflected from the sea is sufficiently circularly polarized, and whether that polarization produces a measurable enantiomeric excess in relevant molecules. Either failure weakens the proposed starting force; success still leaves rival origins of biological homochirality standing.
obstacles: The wording is that asymmetry may have started this way, so a successful laboratory effect does not identify the historical cause.
Parity violation, chance amplification and other chiral biases predict the same biological handedness.
rationale: Only the physical adequacy of a non-living polarizing force is measurable with existing photochemistry and atmospheric optics, and those results sit in papers rather than in one open dataset. Nothing public records the polarization and chemistry of the prebiotic sea surface at the origin of homochirality. The hypothesis is therefore only weakly separable from other asymmetric forces, and only the proxy, not the origin, can be examined now.

operationalization: Compare sectioned pearls, molluscan and teleost otoliths, and albumin-precipitated calcospherites for concentric zoning and radial fabric. A shared geometry supports a common precipitation mode; systematic differences in zoning or crystal habit refute the identification.

candidate_datasets.name: AFORO
candidate_datasets.role: Open catalogue of teleost sagitta images and outlines, a partial view of otolith form rather than sectioned internal fabric.

candidate_datasets.name: MorphoSource
candidate_datasets.role: Downloadable micro-CT of biomineral specimens, usable where otolith or concretion volumes resolve internal zonation.

obstacles: Pearls and artificial calcospherites are mostly illustrated in papers, not in the otolith catalogues.
Similar concentric-radiate structure can arise from more than one precipitation chemistry.
rationale: The structural comparison is measurable, but the inference from shared structure to a shared physico-chemical mode is one interpretation among others. Otolith outlines are well archived, while matched sections of pearls, otoliths and laboratory calcospherites are not. A subset comparison is feasible from images and scans; it would not cleanly exclude other ways of building the same fabric.

operationalization: For scales, otoliths, bones and starch grains with known-age or known-environment series, test whether zone counts match day, season or other external periods. Zones that form without a matching external cycle support the claim that periodicity need not be external; a universal match would refute that caution.

candidate_datasets.name: PANGAEA
candidate_datasets.role: Published sclerochronology and otolith series that pair increment measurements with age or environmental time series.

obstacles: An endogenous oscillator can still lock to an external cycle, so agreement does not prove external cause.
Starch grains and most bones are poorly represented next to commercial fish otoliths and bivalve or coral bands.
rationale: The empirical content is that rhythmic zones are not necessarily calendars, and known-age hard parts can supply mismatches or matches. Increment series are public but scattered across PANGAEA deposits and papers, and they cover a subset of the structures named. Because the claim is a prohibition on assuming an external cause, one well-documented endogenous case is informative, while entrainment keeps many individual series ambiguous.

operationalization: Compare calcium carbonate and phosphate solubility in intact albumin versus its breakdown products, and test whether mineralization fronts in calcified tissues coincide with proteolysis rather than with carbonic-acid reaction on a more soluble salt. Precipitation tied to protein breakdown, and not to the acid route, would support the claim.
obstacles: No public dataset pairs local proteolysis, protein concentration and mineral appearance in calcifying tissues.
Modern mineralization also depends on phosphate supply and inhibitors, which the two historical mechanisms do not capture.
rationale: The chemical alternative is clear enough to test in vitro and at a mineralization front, but the needed paired measurements are not in an open resource. Older solubility remarks are scattered in the chemical literature and do not cover skeletal tissues at the stated scope. Discriminating the protein-breakdown route from carbonic-acid precipitation, among other controls now known to matter, would require new compiled measurements.

operationalization: Place skeletal elements on a size axis and test whether forms near cell size match surface-tension geometries while large bones match load trajectories, using curvature, junction angles and stress-alignment metrics. A change of regime with size supports the claim; the same controlling geometry at both scales refutes it.

candidate_datasets.name: MorphoSource
candidate_datasets.role: 3D scans spanning vertebrate bones and some small skeletal elements, for comparing form against size.

candidate_datasets.name: DigiMorph
candidate_datasets.role: Public CT slices of vertebrate skeletons whose size and load-bearing architecture can be measured.

obstacles: Surface tension versus muscle and gravity has to be inferred from form, and several mappings are possible.
Phylogeny and material change with size, and cell-sized spicules are scarce in CT archives built for bones.
rationale: Scale is measurable and the two regimes suggest different geometries, but the forces themselves are an interpretation of those geometries. Open scans cover large bones well and minute skeletons poorly, so only a biased slice of the size range can be compared. Even a clean size trend would leave material and ancestry as alternative explanations of the form difference.

operationalization: Reconstruct the spicule axis and test whether geodesic curvature on a spherical or ellipsoidal cell surface is indistinguishable from zero, predicting circular, elliptic or helical arcs. Systematic departure from a surface geodesic, or a fit only after implausible cell shapes are assumed, would refute the confinement rule.

candidate_datasets.name: World Porifera Database
candidate_datasets.role: Public taxonomic catalogue with linked sources for curved sponge spicules whose axes can be digitized from images.

candidate_datasets.name: MorphoBank
candidate_datasets.role: Open morphology projects and images that include spicule form for some sponge matrices.

obstacles: The cell surface that confined growth is almost never preserved with the finished spicule.
Many published figures are drawings, and 2D projections underdetermine a space curve.
rationale: A geodesic on a stated surface is a sharp geometric prediction, and C- and S-shaped spicules can be digitized from existing images. What is missing is the cell at the time of growth, so the test becomes a fit to an assumed ellipsoid rather than a measured confinement. That proxy can reject gross mismatches and cannot separate a true geodesic from other curves that also look like circular or spiral arcs.

operationalization: Embed siliceous sponge spicules and calcareous holothurian spicules in a common morphospace and test whether corresponding forms overlap. Overlap supports form set by shared external confinement; separation that tracks mineralogy rather than shape class would refute it.

candidate_datasets.name: World Porifera Database
candidate_datasets.role: Catalogue and linked images of siliceous sponge spicule types used as one side of the comparison.

candidate_datasets.name: World Register of Marine Species
candidate_datasets.role: Taxonomic entry point for holothurians as well as sponges, with links toward species whose spicules are illustrated in the literature.

candidate_datasets.name: MorphoBank
candidate_datasets.role: Morphological matrices and media for coding spicule shape independently of skeletal chemistry.

obstacles: The two groups are not a controlled contrast: cell geometry and ancestry differ along with chemistry.
Quantitative spicule outlines are not in one downloadable table and would have to be measured from plates.
rationale: Form overlap versus mineral class is a fair empirical reading of the argument, and both spicule faunas are extensively illustrated. The illustrations are not a joint morphometric dataset, and holothurian and sponge images sit in different literatures. Similar shapes would still be compatible with convergence for reasons other than cell confinement, so the chemistry-independence claim is only partly separated from its rivals.

operationalization: Measure angles between rays of triradiate and four-rayed spicules. Equal cells should give 120 degree triacts and tetrahedral angles near 109 degrees; a distribution centered on 90 degrees or on no preferred angle would refute the junction rule, and unequal cells should widen that scatter.

candidate_datasets.name: World Porifera Database
candidate_datasets.role: Species-level access to calcareous and tetractinellid sponges whose triact and tetract spicules are illustrated.

candidate_datasets.name: MorphoBank
candidate_datasets.role: Open images and character matrices from which inter-ray angles can be measured for sponge spicules.

obstacles: Most available views are 2D micrographs or drawings, which bias 3D tetrahedral angles.
There is no pre-measured angle table, so the sample has to be compiled from plates.
rationale: The angles are explicit and distinguish the junction hypothesis from orthogonal or random rays. Large numbers of triacts and tetracts have been figured, but they are not an open measurement dataset, and planar triacts are much easier to score than four-rayed spicules in space. A small team could test the 120 degree case from published images; the tetrahedral and unequal-cell clauses need 3D that is only partly available.

operationalization: Measure hexactinellid ray angles for cubic orthogonality versus the angles of closest packing, and, where tissue is preserved, score whether the vesicles around forming spicules are in linear cubic series. Orthogonal rays without cubic vesicle packing would leave the packing mechanism unshown.

candidate_datasets.name: World Porifera Database
candidate_datasets.role: Taxonomic access to hexactinellids and linked spicule illustrations for measuring ray orthogonality.

candidate_datasets.name: MorphoSource
candidate_datasets.role: 3D scans of sponge skeletal elements, sparse for glass sponges but usable where hexactine spicules are deposited.

obstacles: Soft-tissue vesicle packing at the moment of spicule formation is rarely preserved or archived.
Orthogonal silica rays can also be produced by crystal habit, not only by cubic cell packing.
rationale: Ray geometry is scorable from spicule images, but the claim is about the packing of the vesicles that moulded them. Public data are mostly cleaned spicules, not developmental histology, and they cover a modest fraction of hexactinellids in measurable 3D. Orthogonality is compatible with more than one mechanism, so a geometric pass would support only the form half of the claim.

operationalization: From occurrence tables, measure geographic range sizes, sample-level richness and evenness, and the stratigraphic span of families and genera, including whether living taxa are already present in the Cambrian. Cosmopolitan ranges, high local richness without single-species dominance, and Cambrian-to-Recent identity would support the claim; endemic ranges, dominance, or much later first appearances would refute the corresponding clause.

candidate_datasets.name: Neptune Sandbox Berlin archive
candidate_datasets.role: Downloadable deep-sea microfossil occurrences, including radiolarians, for co-occurrence, ranges and stratigraphic duration.

candidate_datasets.name: Ocean Biodiversity Information System
candidate_datasets.role: Living marine occurrence records for testing whether radiolarian species lack geographic limits.

candidate_datasets.name: Paleobiology Database
candidate_datasets.role: Fossil occurrences through the Phanerozoic for testing Cambrian identity and long taxonomic ranges.

obstacles: Sampling effort and taxonomic lumping can mimic cosmopolitanism and high local richness.
Deep-sea drilling archives are strongest in the Cenozoic, so Paleozoic coverage depends on other occurrence compilations.
rationale: Range, dominance and first appearance are standard occurrence statistics, and radiolarians are present in open marine and fossil databases that a small team can query directly. Coverage is uneven between living plankton, deep-sea cores and Paleozoic rocks, but it is enough to confirm or refute worldwide ranges, local diversity and the Cambrian claim. Effort bias is real and is handled by rarefaction rather than by collecting new samples.

operationalization: Compare the grains in agglutinated tests with the surrounding sediment for size, shape and mineralogy, and ask whether the bias matches specific surface energies. A bias predicted by surface energy supports the physical account; a selectivity that surface energy does not predict is at least compatible with active choice.

candidate_datasets.name: PANGAEA
candidate_datasets.role: Sediment grain-size and foraminiferal assemblage tables that can be paired, where co-located, with test composition.

candidate_datasets.name: World Foraminifera Database
candidate_datasets.role: Taxonomic catalogue of agglutinated foraminifera, identifying the species whose grain selection has been described.

obstacles: Grain preference is predicted both by surface energy and by biological selection, so the same bias fits both.
Matched test-plus-sediment measurements are scattered in papers rather than linked in one archive.
rationale: Foreign particles in the test are observable, but volition versus surface energy is not a unique pattern in grain counts. Sediment and foraminiferal census data are public, while the particle-by-particle composition of tests is not systematically attached to them. Existing studies can test a subset of rhizopods and leave the mechanism underdetermined.

operationalization: On spherical lattice shells, measure the fraction of hexagonal meshes, node angles near 120 degrees, and whether irregularity of the mesh tracks irregularity that a vesicular foam would produce. Strong hexagonal order is consistent with groove collection; a different predominant polygon, or order unrelated to any foam, counts against that route.

candidate_datasets.name: Mikrotax
candidate_datasets.role: Image-based taxonomy of Cenozoic radiolarians, including lattice shells whose mesh geometry can be digitized.

obstacles: Finished skeletons do not preserve the surface vesicles that supposedly moulded the grooves.
Hexagonal nets are also expected from other physical models, including bubble packing and reaction-diffusion.
rationale: Mesh statistics are a direct geometric test and radiolarian lattices are extensively imaged in an open taxonomic system. The developmental step, silica collecting in grooves between vesicles, is not in those images. Hexagonal order can therefore support the form prediction for a well-illustrated subset of species while leaving the groove mechanism interchangeable with other pattern-forming processes.

operationalization: Apply one regularity metric, such as mesh-angle variance or deviation from a spherical hex net, to silica radiolarian lattices, strontium-sulphate acantharian skeletons and organic Clathrulina lattices. Equal regularity supports material-independence; regularity that tracks chemistry refutes it.

candidate_datasets.name: Mikrotax
candidate_datasets.role: Open images of radiolarian lattices, the silica side of the comparison, with much thinner coverage of acantharians and heliozoans.

obstacles: Acantharia dissolve and Clathrulina is not a focus of the radiolarian image archives, so the three materials are unequally documented.
Chemistry is confounded with clade, so equal regularity need not mean a shared vesicular mould.
rationale: A common regularity metric across the three named materials is a straightforward test of the independence claim. Silica lattices are well imaged; strontium-sulphate and organic lattices are mostly in separate papers and drawings. The available sample can compare a limited set of species, and phylogenetic confounding keeps a positive result from isolating the mould as the cause.

operationalization: On Callimitra and similar nassellarian skeletons, count interfaces and measure meeting angles against Plateau's laws: faces in threes near 120 degrees and edges near the tetrahedral angle. Agreement supports a four-cell interfacial origin; angles far from those values, or a different topology, refute it.

candidate_datasets.name: Mikrotax
candidate_datasets.role: Radiolarian images and taxonomic plates from which Callimitra-type skeletons can be measured.

obstacles: Many classical figures are schematic, and Haeckel-style drawings can impose the regularity being tested.
Angle agreement does not show that four living cells were present when the skeleton formed.
rationale: The soap-film angles and the tetrahedral graph are specific enough to accept or reject from specimens or faithful images, and the claim is limited to a small group of nassellarians. Public images exist but quantitative 3D of Callimitra is thin, so the testable object is mostly the drawn or photographed geometry. That can confirm the geometric match for this genus and cannot establish the cellular history the geometry is said to require.

operationalization: Measure face regularity of radiolarian pentagonal dodecahedra and icosahedra from specimens or scans. Confirmed regularity excludes an origin in crystallographic space-filling; irregular faces, or only those polyhedra that crystals allow, would remove the stated ground for rejecting a crystallization-like partition.

candidate_datasets.name: Mikrotax
candidate_datasets.role: Images of polyhedral radiolarian skeletons, including circoporid-type forms when figured, for testing face regularity.

obstacles: Thompson's premise relies on Haeckel's figures, which may have been regularized.
These skeletons are uncommon, so a regularity measurement will rest on few specimens.
rationale: Once regularity is measured, the crystallographic restriction does the rest of the work, so the empirical task is whether the dodecahedra and icosahedra are actually regular. Images exist, but they are few, often drawings, and not a 3D morphometric series of Circoporidae. A modern subset can test the geometric premise and cannot by itself rule out every non-crystalline space-partitioning process.

operationalization: Measure the latitudes and counts of the twenty spines. Hexagonal symmetry predicts two polar spines, six equatorial spines and two alternating whorls of six; Müller's arrangement predicts five four-spine circles and no polar spine. A systematic match to one angular template and not the other decides the claim.

candidate_datasets.name: Mikrotax
candidate_datasets.role: Radiolarian skeleton images from which spine positions can be digitized where twenty-spined forms are figured.

obstacles: Acantharia, the main living twenty-spined group, are poorly represented in polycystine image databases and their skeletons are rarely preserved.
Older sources are drawings that may already embody one or the other symmetry scheme.
rationale: The two arrangements make different, quantitative predictions, so spine coordinates would discriminate them cleanly. What is public is a scatter of figures rather than a downloadable angle table, and the best-preserved illustrations are not a random sample of living Acantharia. The test is standard once images are compiled, but current open archives only partly cover the named genera.

operationalization: No outcome cleanly separates an unexplained central polarity, said to be perhaps like fluid-crystal directive forces, from other ways of placing a fixed set of spines. Locating the first sign of polarity in the central cytoplasm would address only that geographical clause.
obstacles: Absence of an obvious mechanical force is not a measurement with a refuting result.
Central origin, cortical origin and several molecular polarities can leave the same adult spine map.
rationale: The passage states that no obvious mechanical account is available and points to fluid crystals as a direction in which to look, which does not fix variables or a decision rule. Adult skeletons show the polarity without showing where it was generated or which force class produced it. Existing images are compatible with the suggestion and with its rivals, so the claim as stated is not an empirical contrast.

operationalization: On cylindrical vessels, tracheids and insect tracheae, classify wall thickenings as annular, longitudinal or helical and test whether helices have constant pitch. All three geodesic families, with constant-pitch helices, support the identification; spirals whose pitch varies along the cell refute the helical geodesic.

candidate_datasets.name: BioImage Archive
candidate_datasets.role: Open microscopy of plant and animal tissues, including xylem and tubular cells whose wall thickenings can be traced.

candidate_datasets.name: Cell Image Library
candidate_datasets.role: Annotated cell images for scoring annular, longitudinal and spiral wall patterns on cylinders.

obstacles: On a cylinder, rings, generators and constant-pitch helices are the geodesics, so the label adds little once the pattern is named.
Quantitative pitch series are sparse compared with textbook illustrations of the three types.
rationale: Occurrence of the three thickening types is standard anatomy and can be checked in public micrographs of vessels and tracheae. Calling them geodesics is then almost a theorem, so the result does not separate the claim from ordinary anatomical description except where pitch is non-constant. Images suffice for a qualitative survey and not for a high-powered discrimination.

operationalization: Unroll or fit the suture and parallel striae of high-spired shells such as Turritella on a cone and test whether they are conical geodesics whose coils tighten toward the apex. A constant-pitch helix, or coils that do not close apically, would refute the stated curve.

candidate_datasets.name: MorphoSource
candidate_datasets.role: 3D scans of gastropod shells from which the sutural curve can be extracted and fit as a geodesic.

candidate_datasets.name: iDigBio
candidate_datasets.role: Specimen photographs of turreted gastropods for measuring how suture spacing changes toward the apex.

candidate_datasets.name: Digital Atlas of Ancient Life
candidate_datasets.role: Open fossil-shell illustrations, including high-spired gastropods, for the same sutural measurement.

obstacles: Photographs give a profile of the suture; a full geodesic test is more secure on 3D scans, which are fewer than photos.
Ornament and repaired breaks can locally displace the suture from the growth curve.
rationale: Tightening coils on a cone are a specific alternative to a constant-pitch helix or to the shell's own logarithmic spiral, and both photographs and scans of Turritella-like shells are public. Coverage is good for common high-spired genera and thinner for the full diversity of turreted forms. Fitting the curve is a standard morphometric job on the order of weeks.

operationalization: Sample reticulated patterns on cell walls and integuments and test what fraction are two opposite constant-pitch helices rather than cracks, vessels or reaction-diffusion nets. A high fraction of crossed geodesics supports the claim that they are a common source; a minority would refute commonness.

candidate_datasets.name: BioImage Archive
candidate_datasets.role: Micrographs of cell surfaces and integuments on which reticula can be classified.

candidate_datasets.name: iDigBio
candidate_datasets.role: Specimen images of organisms whose external reticulate patterns can be sampled, though usually at coarser resolution.

obstacles: Common source requires a defined universe of patterns, and several generators make similar criss-cross textures.
The scope is all curved organic surfaces, far beyond any one image collection.
rationale: Crossed helices can be recognized on individual images, but the claim is about how common that origin is among reticulated patterns. Public images touch pieces of that universe and do not inventory it. Even a careful sample would leave other pattern-forming processes as live alternatives wherever the geometry is only approximately helical.

operationalization: On reconstructed surfaces of heart, stomach, arteries and gut, compare muscle-fiber trajectories with computed geodesics. Fibers lying on shortest paths, annular and longitudinal on a simple tube, support the claim; systematic extra length or a non-geodesic helix would refute it for that organ.

candidate_datasets.name: Human cardiac diffusion MRI dataset
candidate_datasets.role: Open cardiac diffusion-tensor imaging and derived myocardial orientation maps for testing fiber paths against geodesics.

candidate_datasets.name: Cardiac Atlas Project
candidate_datasets.role: Ventricular shape models on which surface geodesics can be computed and compared with fiber directions.

obstacles: Open fiber-orientation data are concentrated on the human left ventricle, not the stomach, arteries, intestine or worm body wall.
Myocardial fibers also follow sheet architecture and load, so a geodesic fit can be confounded with stress alignment.
rationale: Shortest paths on a measured surface are a clear test, and public cardiac diffusion data plus ventricular shape models make the heart part feasible with specialist but existing tools. The claim names a list of hollow organs for which comparable open fiber maps are sparse. A heart-only result would resolve a restricted scope and leave the general automatic-arrangement claim open.

operationalization: Test whether adult heart and stomach fibers are geodesics of the twisted surface, whether oblique gastric fibers match a new pouch geodesic, and whether pump performance requires that shortest-path layout. Adult geodesic fits support only the geometric residue of the developmental claim.

candidate_datasets.name: Human cardiac diffusion MRI dataset
candidate_datasets.role: Adult human myocardial fiber orientations, a proxy for the post-twist heart but not a developmental series.

candidate_datasets.name: Cardiac Atlas Project
candidate_datasets.role: Adult ventricular geometry used to compute geodesics; it does not record the primitive tube or the stomach.

obstacles: Remaining geodetic after twisting requires the fiber map through development, which these adult datasets do not contain.
Effective contraction is compatible with non-geodesic architectures, so function does not isolate the shortest path as necessary.
rationale: The adult heart can be checked for geodesic fibers, which is only the end state of a developmental claim about dilatation, twisting and new gastric systems. Open data are adult ventricular diffusion and shape, not a series from the primitive tube and not a comparable stomach dataset. The further claim that the heart works only because fibers take the shortest course is not separated from other working architectures by these measurements.

operationalization: From 3D tracks, measure body rotation, path curvature and whether the trajectory is a helix about a nearly straight axis rather than a circle. A helix whose turning matches axial rotation supports the swerve-averaging account; circular paths without rotation, or helices produced without body rotation, refute it for that swimmer.

candidate_datasets.name: Dryad bilophotrichous bacterial tracks
candidate_datasets.role: Open 3D swimming trajectories that include helical paths, for a bacterial subset of small swimmers.

candidate_datasets.name: BioImage Archive
candidate_datasets.role: Cell-motility imaging that can supply tracks for additional flagellates and ciliates where deposited.

obstacles: The clearest open 3D tracks are bacteria, whereas the claim centers on ciliates, flagellates, rotifers and swarm-spores.
A helical flagellar beat can draw a helix without a constant body-fixed swerve.
rationale: Helix versus circle, tied to measured body rotation, is a direct and discriminating test, and some open 3D tracks already exist. They represent a slice of small swimmers rather than the full list of ciliated and flagellated organisms. Reanalysis of those tracks is standard; extending the same test to rotifers and typical ciliates depends on imaging that is only partly archived.

operationalization: Fit logarithmic spirals against Archimedean, Fermat and other curves on ruminant horns, mollusc and foraminiferan shells, and sunflower floret parastichies, and fit the cordate leaf outline as the stated exception. A logarithmic spiral uniquely among those forms, and a poor log-spiral fit to the cordate leaf, supports the claim.

candidate_datasets.name: MorphoSource
candidate_datasets.role: 3D shells and some horns whose outlines can be fit to spiral models.

candidate_datasets.name: iDigBio
candidate_datasets.role: Specimen images of shells, leaves and sunflower heads for outline and parastichy fits.

candidate_datasets.name: Mikrotax
candidate_datasets.role: Foraminiferal shell images for the same logarithmic-spiral test.

obstacles: Sunflower parastichies are often treated as Fermat spirals, so the curve family has to be fit rather than assumed.
Horn scans and digitized leaf outlines are less uniformly available than mollusc photographs.
rationale: Competing spiral equations are standard to fit, and public images or scans exist for every class the claim names, including the cordate-leaf exception. Taxonomic depth is greatest for molluscs and thinner for horns and capitula, but a decisive mismatch in any named class would refute the universal. The curve-fitting itself is ordinary morphometrics on existing pictures.

operationalization: The empirical residue is whether a force that turns with the growing body, identified with the columellar muscle in snails, is what produces the spiral, as opposed to an external field of constant direction. That requires force or muscle-activity measurements during growth, not shell outline alone.
obstacles: Shell shape is compatible with any intrinsic asymmetry of growth and does not identify the columellar muscle as the deflecting force.
No public dataset records muscle force through shell coiling.
rationale: That a fixed external direction cannot wind a growing structure into a spiral is a kinematic argument, not a dataset result. The biological claim that the co-rotating force is the columellar muscle needs measurements that have not been archived. Shell collections can show that spirals exist and cannot show which force produced them or exclude other intrinsic growth asymmetries.

operationalization: Along growth lines of tubular shells and horns, measure the ratio of longitudinal to transverse extension and the spiral angle. A ratio that stays constant and matches the angle supports the claim; a drifting ratio that still yields a logarithmic spiral, or a constant ratio that does not, refutes it.

candidate_datasets.name: MorphoSource
candidate_datasets.role: Shell and horn scans with growth increments from which the two rates and the spiral angle can be measured.

candidate_datasets.name: iDigBio
candidate_datasets.role: Photographs of coiled shells whose whorl expansion can be compared with the tangent angle.

obstacles: Horns are less often scanned with usable growth lines than mollusc shells.
Within an ideal logarithmic model the ratio and the angle are linked by definition, so the empirical test is constancy on real specimens.
rationale: Constancy of the growth-rate ratio, and its match to the spiral angle, can be read from increments on existing shells. Public scans and photographs cover common molluscs well enough to accept or reject the relation, with horns as a thinner additional scope. The measurement is standard geometric morphometrics and does not need new collections.

operationalization: On scorpioid cymes, measure successive shoot lengths and divergence angles and test whether the shoots are tangents to a logarithmic spiral. A constant length ratio and equal angles support it; varying ratios that miss the spiral refute it. The helicoid case additionally requires recovering a spiral after removing the twist.

candidate_datasets.name: iDigBio
candidate_datasets.role: Herbarium images of borages and other cymose plants from which shoot lengths and angles can be digitized.

obstacles: Pressed specimens flatten the helicoid twist, so the hidden spiral is not recoverable from a typical sheet.
Shoot lengths are not pre-measured; each inflorescence has to be digitized from a photograph.
rationale: The scorpioid prediction is a concrete length-and-angle pattern, and herbarium photographs of the relevant families are public in large numbers. They are 2D and flattened, so they can test the scorpioid tangent spiral and not the claim that a helicoid cyme hides the same curve. Digitizing a sample is feasible but is compilation rather than a ready-made analysis.

operationalization: Compare shape of successive whorls or growth stages of spiral shells, horns and other terminally accreted structures, scaling them to the same size. Persistent shape supports growth without change of form; systematic ontogenetic allometry refutes it.

candidate_datasets.name: MorphoSource
candidate_datasets.role: 3D shells and horns on which successive whorls can be scaled and compared.

candidate_datasets.name: iDigBio
candidate_datasets.role: Large photographic samples of coiled shells for an ontogenetic shape test.

obstacles: Aperture damage and sculpture can masquerade as shape change.
Some groups are photographed mostly as adults, so early whorls are less often measurable.
rationale: Isometry of successive increments is a standard outline comparison, and shells with visible whorls are abundant in open image and scan collections. The claim is general for spiral shells and similar terminal growth, and the public sample is broad enough that widespread allometry would refute it while widespread isometry would support it. The analysis is routine geometric morphometrics.

operationalization: For shells, opercula, foraminiferal chambers, horns and tusks, test whether each growth increment is a scaled copy of the whole pre-existing outline. Increments that leave the enlarged form similar support the gnomon claim; increments that change the shape refute it.

candidate_datasets.name: MorphoSource
candidate_datasets.role: Scans of accreted hard parts with growth boundaries that can be tested for gnomonic similarity.

candidate_datasets.name: Digital Atlas of Ancient Life
candidate_datasets.role: Illustrated fossil shells and chambers for comparing each added increment with the previous whole.

obstacles: Gnomonic growth is mathematically close to the logarithmic spiral, so the test largely travels with the self-similarity test.
Ornament and repaired shell are additions that are not similar copies and have to be treated explicitly.
rationale: Whether each added piece leaves a similar whole is decidable from growth lines on the same scans and plates used for spiral fits. Coverage of molluscan shells and many fossil chambers is good; tusks and opercula are patchier but not absent. The criterion is close to continued similarity, yet a concrete increment can still fail it, and the measurement is standard.

operationalization: Fit logarithmic spirals to accretionary hard parts (shell, tusk, horn, claw) and to structures built all at once (leaf margins, fish outlines). Better unique fits, usually with growth lines, in the first class, and poor fits in the second, support the prediction.

candidate_datasets.name: MorphoSource
candidate_datasets.role: 3D shells, horns, tusks and claws for logarithmic-spiral fits on accreted parts.

candidate_datasets.name: iDigBio
candidate_datasets.role: Herbarium leaves and other simultaneous outlines used as the predicted negative cases.

candidate_datasets.name: FishBase
candidate_datasets.role: Fish photographs whose body contours can be tested as outlines that should not be logarithmic spirals.

obstacles: Some leaf margins and fin outlines can approximate a spiral over a short arc, so the test needs a pre-set fit criterion.
Claws and tusks are less densely archived than shells.
rationale: The prediction is a contrast between two observable classes, and public images exist for shells, leaves and fish, with scans for many hard parts. Coverage is uneven for claws and tusks but sufficient to populate both sides of the contrast. Accepting or rejecting a logarithmic fit against alternative curves is a standard analysis.

operationalization: Measure whorl breadth along a radius for Nautilus, ammonoids and spiral gastropods and test for a geometric progression, including the specific claim that a Nautilus whorl is about three times the previous one. A constant ratio supports the logarithmic spiral; a drifting or arithmetic series refutes it.

candidate_datasets.name: MorphoSource
candidate_datasets.role: CT and mesh models of nautiloids, ammonoids and gastropods for whorl-breadth series.

candidate_datasets.name: Digital Atlas of Ancient Life
candidate_datasets.role: Scaled fossil-shell photographs from which successive whorl breadths can be measured.

candidate_datasets.name: iDigBio
candidate_datasets.role: Additional specimen images of spiral shells for the same radial measurements.

obstacles: Early whorls are often hidden or crushed, so the series may start mid-growth.
Photographic scale and oblique views add error, smaller on CT than on plates.
rationale: A geometric series of whorl breadths is a direct measurement with a numerical Nautilus benchmark, and open photographs and scans cover nautiloids, ammonoids and many gastropods. The sample is not every species, but it is large enough to confirm or refute both the progression and the threefold Nautilus ratio. The arithmetic is ordinary and can be done in days to weeks.

operationalization: Fit each univalve shell with the generating curve, its expansion, rotation about the pole, translation along the axis and inclination, and test whether residuals between shells are only quantitative. Small residuals support the claim that all form differences are of degree; structured residuals that need extra factors refute that completeness.

candidate_datasets.name: MorphoSource
candidate_datasets.role: 3D univalve shells for fitting the growth-ratio parameters and inspecting residuals.

candidate_datasets.name: iDigBio
candidate_datasets.role: Broad photographic coverage of gastropod and cephalopod shells for the same parameter fit.

candidate_datasets.name: Digital Atlas of Ancient Life
candidate_datasets.role: Fossil univalves, including irregular forms, used to see whether the parameter set still suffices.

obstacles: Sculpture, aperture deviations and uncoiling may sit outside the listed factors, so the residual test depends on how the generating curve is defined.
Open 3D coverage is uneven across living and fossil univalves.
rationale: The parameter list maps onto the usual coiling model and can be fit to public shells, but all differences is stronger than a good fit to typical spires. Irregular, highly sculptured and heteromorph shells are present in the archives yet not in one harmonized morphospace. A large subset can show whether residuals are negligible, without exhausting every difference of form the claim includes.

operationalization: Estimate the logarithmic-spiral constant angle for Nautilus, ammonoids and typical spiral gastropods. A Nautilus angle near 80 degrees, and a distribution for the other shells seldom below 80 and usually 80 to 85 degrees, supports the claim; a substantially lower or broader distribution refutes it.

candidate_datasets.name: MorphoSource
candidate_datasets.role: 3D coiled shells for estimating the tangent angle of the spiral.

candidate_datasets.name: iDigBio
candidate_datasets.role: Photographs of Nautilus, ammonoids and gastropods for a broad angle sample.

candidate_datasets.name: Digital Atlas of Ancient Life
candidate_datasets.role: Fossil cephalopod and gastropod plates used to extend the angle sample through time.

obstacles: The angle is sensitive to which radius and which growth stage is measured when coiling changes.
What counts as a typical spiral gastropod has to be fixed before the 80 to 85 degree band is tested.
rationale: The numerical band is unambiguous and is estimated from the same whorl measurements that test geometric expansion. Public images and scans cover Nautilus and a wide range of ammonoids and gastropods at a sample size that can reject an 80 to 85 degree norm. The calculation is standard once outlines are digitized.

operationalization: Measure the outer-to-inner growth-rate ratio from growth increments independently of the adult outline, and predict whether whorls stand apart, touch or overlap, including the Nautilus pompilius versus N. umbilicatus contrast. A match supports the claim; overlap that disagrees with the increment ratio refutes it.

candidate_datasets.name: MorphoSource
candidate_datasets.role: Shell volumes in which growth lines and umbilical overlap can be measured separately.

candidate_datasets.name: iDigBio
candidate_datasets.role: Photographs of open and closed spirals, stronger for outline overlap than for independent increment rates.

obstacles: Inside the logarithmic model, overlap is largely fixed by the expansion ratio, so an outline-only test is nearly geometric rather than empirical.
Many photographs do not resolve the increments needed for an independent rate.
rationale: Open, touching and overlapping whorls are easy to score, and both nautiloid conditions are represented in public collections. A non-circular test needs the inner and outer rates from growth lines, which scans provide for a subset and ordinary photos often do not. Where only the outline is used, the result mostly restates the spiral geometry instead of discriminating a biological mechanism.

operationalization: Compare spiral angle with phylogenetic distance or ancestral states estimated without using coiling as a character. If angle does not predict which form is ancestral or intermediate, the claim that it is not evidence of ancestry is supported; a robust phylogenetic signal would refute that denial.

candidate_datasets.name: Paleobiology Database
candidate_datasets.role: Fossil cephalopod occurrences and taxonomy used to place shell forms in time without treating the angle as a character.

candidate_datasets.name: Open Tree of Life
candidate_datasets.role: Living molluscan phylogenies against which shell angles of extant relatives can be compared.

candidate_datasets.name: MorphoSource
candidate_datasets.role: Shell meshes for measuring the angle that is then compared with an independent tree.

obstacles: Ammonoid cladograms have often used coiling, so a fossil test can become circular.
No evidence of ancestry is an epistemic claim: a weak correlation need not count as valid support, and the threshold is a judgement.
rationale: Living molluscs have trees that do not depend on shell angle, and shell scans can supply the angles, so a restricted test is possible. Fossil series from straight to coiled shells are the historically important case, and there the phylogeny is morphology-heavy. The analysis can show whether angle tracks ancestry in living groups and cannot cleanly vindicate or dismiss the fossil phylogenetic series Thompson rejects.

operationalization: Along fossil and living shell series, test for monotonic change in growth ratios that is not obvious by eye, and test whether similar forms arise in unrelated clades. Independent origins support the convergence warning; a directional ratio trend is compatible with orthogenesis and with selection, so it does not establish orthogenesis.

candidate_datasets.name: Paleobiology Database
candidate_datasets.role: Time-calibrated occurrences of molluscan lineages in which growth-ratio trends can be ordered.

candidate_datasets.name: Open Tree of Life
candidate_datasets.role: Phylogenies for distinguishing shared ancestry from independent origins of similar shell forms.

candidate_datasets.name: MorphoSource
candidate_datasets.role: Shell shape measurements paired with those trees and time series.

obstacles: A morphological trend does not separate an internal orthogenetic drive from selection or sampling.
The claim that a method can help recognise such series is only partly a claim about nature.
rationale: Convergence of shell form is testable by placing similar geometries on independent trees, and the occurrence, tree and scan resources exist for a molluscan subset. Orthogenesis, as a real directed tendency rather than a description of a trend, has no outcome that current data would assign to it instead of to selection. The usable result is therefore the convergence half and the detection of trends, not the causal status of orthogenesis.

operationalization: Measure spiral angle through ontogeny in Oekotraustes, Scaphites, Ancyloceras, Lituites and similar shells. An increasing angle with narrowing whorls, and a decreasing angle toward an open hook, support the claim; constant angle despite those outlines, or the opposite angle trend, refutes it for those taxa.

candidate_datasets.name: MorphoSource
candidate_datasets.role: CT of heteromorph ammonoids where deposited, for ontogenetic angle along the shell.

candidate_datasets.name: Digital Atlas of Ancient Life
candidate_datasets.role: Illustrated ammonoids, including uncoiling forms, for measuring whorl change along the spiral.

candidate_datasets.name: iDigBio
candidate_datasets.role: Museum photographs of the named genera supplying additional ontogenetic profiles.

obstacles: 3D scans of these particular genera are fewer than photographs, and crushed specimens distort the later whorls.
A change in outline can reflect translation or aperture shape as well as the spiral angle.
rationale: The claim names genera and the direction in which the angle should move, and those shells are figured in open museum and atlas collections. Photographs can test the narrowing and uncoiling profiles; scans, where present, separate the angle from other coiling parameters. The sample is uneven but large enough, with standard measurements, to confirm or refute the stated ontogenetic trends.

operationalization: For Cerithium, Solarium (Architectonica), Natica, Planorbis and similar shells, estimate the spiral angle and the apical angle of the enveloping cone. Similar spiral angles with apical angles that track the visible form difference support the claim; large spiral-angle differences among these shells refute it.

candidate_datasets.name: iDigBio
candidate_datasets.role: Photographs of the named gastropod genera for spiral and apical angles.

candidate_datasets.name: MorphoSource
candidate_datasets.role: 3D shells of turbinate and discoid gastropods for the same two angles.

candidate_datasets.name: Digital Atlas of Ancient Life
candidate_datasets.role: Fossil gastropod plates that extend the comparison across the same body forms.

obstacles: Apical angle and spiral angle can be confused on a single photograph if the axis is not in the plane of the picture.
Modern genus limits differ from Thompson's Solarium and Planorbis, so the sample has to follow the shapes he named.
rationale: Both angles are standard shell measurements, and the four body forms are common in public photograph and scan collections. The contrast he draws is quantitative and can be accepted or rejected from a modest sample of each form. Orientation error is manageable on 3D meshes and on well-posed photographs.

operationalization: Digitize growth lines of bivalves and brachiopods, including Anomia, Lima and Solen, and test whether they are coaxial circles, ellipses or other coaxial curves through the umbo rather than concentric curves about a shifting center. A directional growth function is then fit to the family of curves; concentric lines, or no single coaxial family, refute the geometric claim.

candidate_datasets.name: iDigBio
candidate_datasets.role: Photographs of bivalves with visible growth lines for fitting coaxial versus concentric models.

candidate_datasets.name: Digital Atlas of Ancient Life
candidate_datasets.role: Fossil bivalve and brachiopod plates showing growth lines through the umbo.

candidate_datasets.name: MorphoSource
candidate_datasets.role: 3D shells for growth-line geometry when surface relief is hard to read in photographs.

obstacles: Several directional functions can generate similar coaxial families, so the simplest-function clause is less sharp than the coaxial geometry.
Abraded umbones hide the point the curves should share.
rationale: Coaxial versus concentric growth lines are visually and numerically distinguishable, and the named genera are well represented by open photographs. The directional-growth interpretation is a further fit, but the geometric pattern itself can confirm or refute the main statement. Measuring curves on existing images is standard and does not require new specimens.

operationalization: On Estheria and similar conchostracans, test whether surface lines are edges of retained moults, visible in section as stacked carapaces, and whether the outline is a logarithmic spiral of small angle. Stacked retained valves support the incomplete-moult mechanism; a single accreted sheet with growth lines would refute it.

candidate_datasets.name: iDigBio
candidate_datasets.role: Specimen images of clam shrimps for outline spirals and surface lines of growth.

candidate_datasets.name: Digital Atlas of Ancient Life
candidate_datasets.role: Fossil conchostracan illustrations used for the same outline and growth-line comparison.

obstacles: External lines alone cannot separate retained moults from true shell accretion; that needs sections, which are mostly in papers.
Estheria has been split among several modern genera, so the specimen set has to be delimited carefully.
rationale: The outline spiral and the presence of marginal lines can be scored from museum photographs of a narrow group of crustaceans, which are present in public collections. The mechanism, incomplete moulting with a new carapace under the old one, is decided by cross-sections that are not assembled as a dataset. Photographs therefore test the mollusc-like geometry and only proxy the moult interpretation.

operationalization: Pair brachidial spiral direction and form with shell outline across spire-bearing brachiopods: outward spirals with transverse shells such as Spirifer, inward spirals with rounded shells such as Atrypa, and discoid spirals with flattened shells. The association is supported or refuted by that cross-tabulation; the pressure mechanism remains an interpretation of the association.

candidate_datasets.name: Digital Atlas of Ancient Life
candidate_datasets.role: Illustrated brachiopods, some with spiralia, for pairing shell shape with spiral direction.

candidate_datasets.name: MorphoSource
candidate_datasets.role: CT of brachiopods in which internal spiral brachidia are visible.

candidate_datasets.name: Paleobiology Database
candidate_datasets.role: Taxonomic and occurrence framework for the spire-bearing groups being compared.

obstacles: Spiral direction and shell shape can be conserved together by ancestry rather than by spatial constraint.
Many specimens preserve the shell outline without the brachidium, so the paired sample is smaller than shell collections.
rationale: The predicted association of spiral direction with shell shape is checkable from illustrated and scanned brachiopods, and those resources exist for the classical genera. They do not record the pressures inside the shell, so the causal clause is not directly measured. Phylogenetic conservatism can produce the same association, which limits how far a positive table would establish the mechanical explanation.

operationalization: Compare aptychus microstructure, growth and position with ammonoid shells, Nautilus, Sepia, Spirula and thecosome pteropods under explicit homology criteria for a split cone. Shared growth and shell microstructure would support the united-cone hypothesis; jaw- or operculum-like structure and a mismatch with Sepia or Spirula would count against it.

candidate_datasets.name: Paleobiology Database
candidate_datasets.role: Occurrences and taxonomy of ammonoids, aptychi and other cephalopods used to place the structures being compared.

candidate_datasets.name: MorphoSource
candidate_datasets.role: 3D scans of cephalopod shells and, where present, aptychi, for shape comparison with pteropod and sepiid shells.

candidate_datasets.name: Digital Atlas of Ancient Life
candidate_datasets.role: Illustrated ammonoids and aptychi for growth-line and outline comparison.

obstacles: Homology criteria for extinct hard parts are contested, so the same specimens can be scored for more than one identification.
Ammonites provide no developmental series that could show a cone splitting into shell and aptychus.
rationale: Specimens and images of aptychi, ammonoid shells and the living analogues exist in open collections, so microstructure and position can be compared for a subset. Thompson frames the idea as a suspicion, and several homology schemes remain compatible with the same fossils. The data can damage or mildly support the split-cone reading and cannot reconstruct the unobserved united shell.

operationalization: From CT of nautiloid and ammonoid septa, estimate mean curvature given the suture as boundary, and compare spherical, ellipsoidal and saddle cases with the attachment Thompson describes. Near-zero mean curvature supports a minimal surface; systematic mean curvature, or a better fit by a non-minimal shell, refutes it.

candidate_datasets.name: MorphoSource
candidate_datasets.role: Micro-CT of chambered cephalopod shells from which septal surfaces and their boundaries can be meshed.

candidate_datasets.name: Digital Atlas of Ancient Life
candidate_datasets.role: Suture outlines and sectioned shells used to classify attachment geometry where full septal scans are lacking.

obstacles: Downloadable CT is richer for Nautilus and a few ammonoids than for the full range of orthocones and suture types.
A thin elastic membrane under pressure is minimal only under the isotropy and uniform-pressure assumptions.
rationale: Mean curvature of a septal mesh, with the suture as the boundary condition, is a direct test of the soap-film claim, and public CT of chambered shells is sufficient to run it on a real sample. Coverage does not include every septal type, but the spherical, oblique and saddle cases are represented well enough to confirm or refute the geometry. Meshing and curvature are specialist but standard and can be done in weeks to a few months.

operationalization: Quantify the fine branching of ammonitic sutures, including rounded terminal arcs, and compare those statistics with surface-tension fingering patterns and with buckling or wrinkling alternatives. A unique match to surface-tension geometry would support the claim; an equal or better match to another generator would leave it unresolved.

candidate_datasets.name: Digital Atlas of Ancient Life
candidate_datasets.role: Ammonoid suture illustrations from which lobe and fringe geometry can be traced.

candidate_datasets.name: MorphoSource
candidate_datasets.role: 3D ammonoids whose suture lines can be extracted from the shell surface rather than from drawings.

obstacles: Rounded, arborescent outlines are produced by several interfacial instabilities, not only by surface tension.
Classical suture drawings emphasize the pattern the claim treats as diagnostic.
rationale: Suture frills can be measured from open plates and scans, so the descriptive pattern is accessible for complex ammonitic sutures. Identifying that pattern as surface tension, by analogy with milk on a greasy plate or oil on alkali, does not specify a statistic that excludes buckling and other branching processes. Existing images can test the geometry and cannot isolate the physical cause.

operationalization: Place gastropod, cephalopod, foraminiferal and tube-worm shells in one coiling morphospace and test recurrence of the same forms across clades, geological periods and climate or depth settings. Repeated overlap, with forms mixed within deposits, supports the claim; forms restricted to clade, era or climate refute the corresponding part.

candidate_datasets.name: Paleobiology Database
candidate_datasets.role: Phanerozoic occurrences of molluscs, foraminifera and tube-dwelling worms for time, geography and co-occurrence.

candidate_datasets.name: MorphoSource
candidate_datasets.role: 3D shells for mathematical comparison of coiling across groups, strongest for molluscs.

candidate_datasets.name: Mikrotax
candidate_datasets.role: Foraminiferal images so that coiled foraminifera can enter the same morphospace as mollusc shells.

obstacles: A common measurement protocol for molluscs, foraminifera and worm tubes is not already computed, and worm tubes are sparsely scanned.
Preservation and sampling differ by period and climate, which can create false recurrences or hide real habitat limits.
rationale: Occurrences through time and shell images are both public, so recurrence of coiled forms among molluscs, and their mixing in faunas, can be tested now. Extending mathematically identical to foraminifera and tube worms, in every period and irrespective of climate, needs a harmonized morphospace that only partly exists. That is months of alignment rather than a single standard analysis, and it would still leave sampling bias in the fossil record.

operationalization: No measurement of shell form distinguishes growth ratios that made selection unnecessary from growth ratios that selection had already shaped. Showing that coiling follows from growth ratios restates the geometry and does not test whether selection had a necessary share.
obstacles: Any observed set of growth ratios is compatible both with selection on those ratios and with selection playing no necessary part.
Widening natural selection to any filter that makes some forms common, as the text itself notes, removes the biological contrast.
rationale: The claim denies that natural selection, in a strictly biological sense, is needed to produce spiral shell diversity, while granting that the forms follow from growth rates. Shell morphospaces can describe those rates and cannot show that selection was unnecessary in producing them. Every plausible distribution of forms fits both the claim and its rival, so the denial has no separating empirical consequence.
